newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ballooning S. Africa credit a headache for banks.
newsitem.headline: Ballooning S. Africa credit a headache for banks.

text.p: Excessive credit extension is a growing worry for South African monetary authorities and commercial banks, and industry observers see no immediate respite for hard-pressed borrowers.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals warned on Tuesday that high levels of private credit extension had to be reduced and said the situation cast a shadow over banks' loan books.
Luke Doig, senior economist at credit insurance firm Credit Guarantee, said the credit situation of individuals was now a matter of concern.
"The absolute levels of household debt and default judgements are extremely high," he said.
The value of debt judgements against private individuals rose 31.7 percent in the first half of this year to 1.47 billion rand from the corresponding period last year.
At the same time, many firms were "teetering on the edge" in terms of having to raise loan finance just to meet their day-to-day requirements, he said.
"We could have a very rapid deterioration in insolvencies and liquidations towards the latter part of the year."
Stals fired a warning to banks in his address to the central bank's annual meeting on Tuesday, urging them to apply greater caution in lending.

"The stage has been reached where the average South African household has to earmark almost six weeks' of its annual income for the sole purpose of servicing the cost of its debt," Stals said. "This situation also casts some doubt on the quality of the loan book of banking institutions."

European credit rating agency IBCA director for banking Mark Young said a much larger proportion of the new South Africa was now being drawn into the banking sector, possibly fuelling the credit growth.
But he remained relatively sanguine about prospects for banks at present.

"There are no alarm bells yet. Our banks are well capitalised and have relatively high provisions. But if the level of savings keeps on dropping, it is obviously a concern and may contribute to a slowdown of lending growth," he said.
Banking sector analysts said the situation had been aggravated by mushrooming credit offers from retailers.

But they said the big banks themselves had put aside fairly large amounts in terms of provisions for bad debt and the high level of credit extension was therefore unlikely to affect financial results.
There is little light at the end of the tunnel for borrowers, however, with Stals indicating no near-term cut in interest rates.

South Africa's key Bank rate currently stands at 16 percent while prime is at 19.50 percent. With consumer inflation running at just over seven percent, that gives South Africa one of the highest real rates of interest in the world.
